system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

Each turn shows the current state of the investigation, including what you already tried. Do not repeat a call listed there.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they value convenience, cost savings, and the ability to manage their own laundry, leading to higher purchase rates and willingness to pay a premium.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain independence and lower utility bills; Electron‑x gains consumer revenue and brand awareness.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing demand for home‑laundry independence and the perception of cost savings drive homeowners to choose consumer‑operated solutions over traditional utility services.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electron‑x can capture value through premium pricing, subscription services for additional features, and data monetization from usage patterns.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for convenience and cost savings.
The supply of Electron‑x consumer‑operated units meets demand.
Regulatory and safety standards allow consumer‑operated units to be installed in residential buildings.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate high intent to purchase a consumer‑operated unit within the next 12 months.
Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional unit.
Pilot deployment in a residential building will achieve at least 30% occupancy rate.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Small businesses prioritize equipment that minimizes downtime and maintenance costs, and consumer‑operated units meet these needs while offering a lower upfront cost than professional models.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electron‑x can capture value through volume sales, bundled accessories, and data services that provide insights into usage patterns and equipment health.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging the growing residential demand for commercial‑quality home laundry solutions. Begin with a limited pilot of a compact, consumer‑operated unit to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions if they perceive them as convenient and cost‑effective, leading to higher purchase rates and willingness to pay a premium.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking convenient laundry options and Electron‑x, which gains new revenue streams and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Convenience reduces time spent on laundry; cost‑effectiveness lowers monthly expenses compared to renting a laundromat or hiring a service.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can sell integrated consumer‑operated units at retail or wholesale prices, capturing margin on hardware and service contracts.
assumptions: Homeowners currently lack convenient, affordable laundry options at home.
They are willing to invest in a consumer‑operated unit despite higher upfront cost.
Electrolux can produce a compact, reliable unit that fits home spaces.
predictions: In a test offering a compact consumer‑operated unit to homeowners, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than a control group receiving a standard professional unit.
Surveyed homeowners will cite convenience and cost savings as primary purchase drivers.

X1.name: Consumer vs Business Messaging Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two product descriptions: one for a consumer‑operated unit (home laundry) and one for a business‑operated unit (small business). They then indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7‑point scale. The test runs in two parallel groups, each receiving the corresponding product description.
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 homeowners (recruited via residential panels) and 100 small‑business decision‑makers (recruited via B2B panels). Randomly assigned to each product group.
X1.measure: Average WTP and purchase intent (on 7‑point scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will report higher WTP and purchase intent for the consumer‑operated unit than for the business unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small‑business decision‑makers will report higher WTP and purchase intent for the business‑operated unit than for the consumer unit.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address homeowner demand, purchase intent, or willingness to pay for consumer‑operated laundry solutions. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging the growing residential demand for commercial‑quality home laundry solutions. Begin with a limited pilot of a compact, consumer‑operated unit to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners seeking convenient, affordable laundry options for multi‑family buildings, student housing, or other residential settings.
final.value_proposition: A compact, reliable consumer‑operated unit that delivers commercial‑grade performance, convenience, and cost‑effectiveness, enabling homeowners to run their own laundry without rental or service contracts.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Business Messaging Test (200 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for the consumer‑operated unit versus a business‑operated unit.
final.uncertainty: The size of the residential market and the actual willingness to pay a premium for convenience and cost‑effectiveness are uncertain. The test will clarify whether homeowners will adopt the consumer proposition.
would_change_if: If the test shows the consumer unit’s average willingness to pay is at least 1.5 points higher than the business unit and purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher, we would proceed to develop and launch the consumer proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or the business unit outperforms, we would reconsider expansion and focus on the professional segment or other alternatives.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions if they perceive them as a convenient, cost‑effective alternative to traditional laundromats, and if they trust the brand for reliability.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain convenience and lower utility bills; Electron‑x gains a new revenue stream and brand exposure in residential markets.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing home‑laundry frequency and awareness of utility costs create demand for self‑service options; brand trust and reliability reduce perceived risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electron‑x can price a consumer‑grade unit at a premium over professional models, sell through retail channels, and capture recurring service revenue.
assumptions: Homeowners are willing to purchase a consumer‑grade laundry solution for a single unit.
Electron‑x’s brand reputation for professional quality transfers to residential products.
Regulatory and safety standards for residential units are met and do not differ significantly from professional units.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate intent to purchase a consumer‑grade unit within 12 months at a price 15‑10% above professional units.
Pilot sales of a consumer‑grade unit in a retail store will achieve at least 5 units per month after 3 months, meeting a 15‑10% conversion rate.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience.
arguments.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.
assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.
A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.
Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.
Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.
Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, low‑maintenance solution that reduces the hassle of bottled water or other alternative water sources.
arguments.who_benefits: Busy households and consumers who currently spend time and money on bottled water, delivery services, or other water alternatives.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If Aquaporin offers a membrane that is easy to install, requires minimal maintenance (e.g., cartridge replacement indicator), and integrates with smart home systems, consumers will switch from the hassle of bottled water to a single, self‑s
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Lower upfront cost compared to premium membrane, subscription services for maintenance, and data‑driven insights that enhance convenience through smart home integration.
assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.
A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.
Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.
Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher repeat purchase rates than standard membranes.
Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.

Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).

3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

X1.name: Messaging Test: Premium vs Convenience Messaging
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with between‑subjects design. Participants view two versions of a product description (premium vs convenience) for the same membrane. They select which version they would purchase and indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and perceived importance of attributes (taste, safety, convenience, maintenance).
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a representative Danish population.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary: would purchase premium vs convenience version). Secondary outcomes: WTP (max price participants would pay) and importance ratings (1‑10).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher WTP than convenience messaging, because health‑enhancing positioning aligns with T1’s claim that premium perception drives adoption.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher WTP than premium messaging, because low‑maintenance positioning aligns with T2’s claim that convenience reduces perceived effort and drives adoption.

X1.decision_rule: If premium messaging achieves at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than convenience messaging, and the difference in WTP is at least €10, then T1 is supported and a differentiated premium consumer proposition is justified.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience, particularly in Denmark and potentially other markets where tap water quality is perceived as uncertain.
final.value_proposition: A high‑performance membrane that eliminates taste concerns, provides clear health benefits, and offers easy installation and low maintenance, enabling premium pricing and subscription services for maintenance.
final.next_action: Run the proposed messaging test (500 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare premium vs. convenience messaging and determine whether premium positioning drives higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: The size of the premium‑willing segment, actual willingness to pay, and the ability to scale production and distribution remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand for a differentiated proposition is needed before committing resources.
would_change_if: If the messaging test shows convenience messaging achieving at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent and a €10 price premium, or if a survey reveals that taste/safety is the primary barrier to tap water use, we would shift focus
to a convenience‑focused proposition and explore low‑upfront‑cost models.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium taste, safety, and health benefits, targeting health‑conscious consumers who currently avoid tap water due to perceived risks or taste concerns.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience.
T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.
assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.
A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.
Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.
Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.
Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings.

assumptions: Consumers currently find bottled water delivery inconvenient or expensive.
A low‑maintenance membrane reduces perceived effort.
Smart home compatibility can be marketed as a convenience benefit.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.

Pilot units will achieve higher adoption rates in households with children or elderly members.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, health‑enhancing solution that addresses specific concerns such as taste, safety, or convenience.
T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.
assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.
A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.
Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.
Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.
Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings.

X1.name: Membrane Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios
X1.sample: 500 Danish adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a differentiated membrane (premium taste/health vs. low‑maintenance convenience) and self‑reported primary reason for choosing the membrane.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group receiving premium positioning will show WTP at least 20% higher than the low‑maintenance group, and will cite taste or health concerns as primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group receiving low‑maintenance positioning will show WTP at least 20% higher than the premium group, and will cite convenience or reduced effort as primary reason.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test SYN-D concerns packing errors and does not address consumer perception of premium taste/health benefits, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience, particularly in Denmark and potentially other markets where tap water quality is perceived as uncertain.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated membrane that delivers superior taste, clear health benefits, and easy installation/maintenance, positioned as a premium home purifier that reduces reliance on bottled water.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Membrane Preference Test (500 Danish adults, three groups, willingness to pay and primary reason for choosing). Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a premium positioning pilot.
final.uncertainty: The size of the premium‑positioning premium over low‑maintenance convenience is unknown; consumer willingness to pay for taste/health benefits is not quantified; market size for a differentiated unit is uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows low‑maintenance convenience WTP at least 20% higher than premium taste/health WTP, or if a survey reveals convenience as the primary reason for choosing a membrane, we would shift focus to a low‑maintenance proposition.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: If Aquaporin positions its membrane as a high‑performance, easy‑to‑use purifier that eliminates taste concerns and provides clear health benefits, consumers will shift from bottled water to a single, reliable home unit.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing for a differentiated unit, subscription services for maintenance, and brand extension into lifestyle segments.
assumptions: Consumers currently avoid tap water due to taste or safety concerns.
A premium positioning can overcome these barriers.
Aquaporin can scale production and distribution to meet demand.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a membrane that promises superior taste and health benefits.
Pilot sales of a differentiated unit will show higher conversion rates than standard membranes.
Brand perception surveys will rank the differentiated unit higher than current offerings.

predictions: Surveyed consumers will rank convenience as a top reason for choosing a membrane over bottled water.

X1.name: Membrane Positioning Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel in Denmark and Germany, balanced by age, gender, and household income.
X1.measure: Average WTP (€) for a differentiated membrane that promises either premium taste/health benefits (T1) or low‑maintenance convenience (T2). Secondary measure: self‑reported current water‑source preference (tap vs bottled vs other).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP for the premium positioning will be at least 20% higher than the baseline (€30) when taste/health benefits are emphasized.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP for the convenience positioning will be at least 20% higher than the baseline (€30) when low‑maintenance features are emphasized.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium positioning WTP exceeds €40, proceed to develop a differentiated membrane targeting health‑conscious consumers; if the convenience positioning WTP exceeds €40, develop a differentiated membrane targeting convenience‑driven

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing errors and does not address consumer perception of premium positioning, taste, safety, or convenience. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the membrane as a premium, health‑enhancing solution addressing taste, safety, and convenience concerns. Begin with a limited pilot in a niche segment (e.g., health‑conscious households) to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious consumers who currently rely on bottled water or prefer a premium water experience.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated membrane that promises superior taste, safety, and health benefits, delivered with easy installation and low maintenance, positioned as a premium home water purifier.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Membrane Positioning Test (300 consumers, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to pay for premium positioning versus convenience positioning.
final.uncertainty: The size of the premium‑positioning premium and the actual demand for a differentiated unit remain uncertain; evidence of strong consumer preference for premium positioning is needed.
would_change_if: If the test shows willingness to pay for premium positioning below €40, we would reconsider the premium positioning and focus on convenience or no expansion.
If a separate test shows strong demand for low‑maintenance convenience, we would develop a convenience‑focused proposition instead.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).

4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group (through higher margins and brand prestige) and home barista enthusiasts who value quality and social experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The pandemic reinforced the home barista lifestyle, creating a cultural shift where coffee is enjoyed at home for social and personal enjoyment, not just for quick consumption.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can price equipment at premium levels, sell through specialty retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, and leverage its brand reputation to command higher prices.
assumptions: Home barista culture will persist beyond the pandemic.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for high-quality espresso equipment.
Simonelli can effectively communicate the premium value to consumers.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can sell equipment through specialty retailers or directly to shops, leveraging its professional reputation to command premium prices and build loyalty among shop owners.
assumptions: Professional coffee shops will maintain or increase spending on equipment.

Simonelli can effectively communicate professional credentials to both shops and consumers.

X1.name: Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product launch. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) premium, home-barista focus (emphasizing quality, social experience, and personal enjoyment) or (B) professional, shop-focused (emphasizing brand prestige, professional standards, and shop compatibility). Participants view a product description of a new consumer espresso machine (e.g., compact, easy
X1.sample: 400 participants: 200 assigned to Condition A, 200 assigned to Condition B. Recruit via coffee enthusiast panels and social media to ensure diversity in age, gender, and coffee consumption habits.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary: would buy), brand perception (Likert scale), and intent to recommend to peers.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition A (home-barista messaging) than in Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition B (professional messaging) than in Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average WTP between the two conditions is at least €20 (indicating Condition A is significantly more willing to pay) and the purchase intent difference is at least 15 percentage points in favor of Condition A, proceed

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home barista enthusiasts, leveraging premium positioning and direct-to-consumer channels. Begin with a limited launch of a compact, high-quality espresso machine and build brand awareness through specialty retailers and social media.
final.target_customer: Home barista enthusiasts who enjoy coffee at home for social and personal enjoyment, and who value quality and brand.
final.value_proposition: A premium, compact espresso machine that combines professional performance with a user-friendly design, positioned as the ultimate home barista tool for personal enjoyment and social sharing.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full product launch.
final.uncertainty: The long-term sustainability of home barista culture and consumer willingness to pay a premium for espresso equipment remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product launch. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) premium, home-barista focus (emphasizing quality, social experience, and personal enjoyment) or (B) professional, shop-focused (emphasizing brand prestige, professional standards, and shop compatibility). Participants view a product description of a new consumer espresso machine (e.g., compact, easy
arguments.sample: 400 participants: 200 assigned to Condition A, 200 assigned to Condition B. Recruit via coffee enthusiast panels and social media to ensure diversity in age, gender, and coffee consumption habits.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary: would buy), brand perception (Likert scale), and intent to recommend to peers.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition A (home-barista messaging) than in Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition B (professional messaging) than in Condition A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in average WTP between the two conditions is at least €20 (indicating Condition A is significantly more willing to pay) and the purchase intent difference is at least 15 percentage points in favor of Condition A, proceed

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full product launch.
arguments.uncertainty: The long-term sustainability of home barista culture and consumer willingness to pay a premium for espresso equipment remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and compact design, targeting home baristas who value time efficiency and space savings. Begin with a limited launch of a compact, quick-brewing machine priced at €2,000‑€2,500, using existing marketing channels to communicate convenience benefits.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Home baristas value convenience and compact design; they will purchase a new consumer machine if it offers quick brewing and easy storage, even at a premium price.
T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher-margin sales and brand association with home convenience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Baristas prioritize time efficiency and space savings in small homes or offices; a compact machine reduces setup time and footprint.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing justified by convenience; Simonelli can capture value through direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning as a home convenience leader.
assumptions: Home barista market exists and is willing to pay for convenience.
Simonelli can produce a compact machine without compromising performance.
Marketing can effectively communicate convenience benefits.
predictions: If offered a compact machine priced at €2,000-€2,500, at least 15% of surveyed home baristas will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher than for a standard professional machine of similar price point.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Premium
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 300 adult home baristas recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and coffee frequency.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy?"), willingness-to-pay (EUR), and perceived importance of convenience vs premium quality.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 15% of respondents will select convenience as the top reason for choosing a new machine, and willingness-to-pay for a compact, quick brewing machine will be above €2,000.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 15% of respondents will select premium quality as the top reason, and willingness-to-pay for a high-performance machine will be above €3,000.

X1.decision_rule: If convenience-driven intent exceeds premium-quality intent by at least 10 percentage points and the average willingness-to-pay for convenience exceeds that for premium by at least €500, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test SYN-D concerns packing errors and does not address consumer demand for convenience or compact design, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and compact design, targeting home baristas who value time efficiency and space savings. Begin with a limited launch of a compact, quick-brewing machine priced at €2,000‑20,000, using existing marketing channels to communicate convenience benefits.
final.target_customer: Home baristas (individuals) who brew espresso at home, especially those with limited space or time.
final.value_proposition: A compact, quick-brewing machine that reduces setup time and footprint, offering convenience without compromising on taste or performance.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (Convenience vs Premium) to validate demand for convenience-driven purchases. If the test meets the decision threshold, proceed to develop and launch the compact machine.
final.uncertainty: The size of the home barista market and willingness to pay for convenience remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.
would_change_if: If the test shows premium-quality demand exceeding convenience demand by at least 10 percentage points and willingness-to-pay for premium exceeds convenience by at least €500, we would shift focus to a premium proposition.
If the test yields no significant difference between convenience and premium intent, we would reconsider the entire consumer expansion strategy.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leading them to purchase premium, smart appliances.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking efficient, health-conscious cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the appliance is marketed as a time-saving, steam‑based cooking system that also offers health benefits (e.g., lower oil use, even cooking), home cooks will shift from traditional methods to a premium, smart device.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can capture value by pricing the product at a premium, selling through retail channels, and offering subscription services for software updates or maintenance.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a premium for convenience and health benefits.

Marketing can effectively communicate the convenience and health benefits to target consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a differentiated home‑cook combi‑steamer at a 20% premium over a standard model, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than a baseline model without premium positioning.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition that emphasizes convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology. Begin with a limited pilot in high‑income German households to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leading them to purchase premium, smart appliances.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking efficient, health-conscious cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the appliance is marketed as a time-saving, steam‑based cooking system that also offers health benefits (e.g., lower oil use, even cooking), home cooks will be willing to pay a premium over traditional methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can capture value by selling a differentiated, branded product at a premium price through direct channels, subscription services, or retail partnerships, leveraging its existing B2B reputation.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay more for convenience and health claims.
Marketing can effectively communicate these benefits to a consumer audience.
The combi-steamer can be adapted to residential use without major redesign.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate intent to purchase a combi-steamer priced 20-30% above a comparable traditional steamer.
Purchase intent will be higher when the product is framed as a health‑enhancing appliance versus a purely convenience appliance.
Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher household income and exposure to premium kitchen appliances.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leading them to purchase premium, smart appliances.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they seek a single, versatile appliance that replaces multiple kitchen tools, reducing clutter and saving space, leading them to purchase a premium, integrated system.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks with limited kitchen space and those who prefer a streamlined, multi‑function appliance.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If the appliance can perform multiple cooking functions (steaming, boiling, sautéing) and is marketed as a space‑saving solution, home cooks will be willing to pay more for a compact, integrated unit that simplifies meal preparation.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can capture value by offering a premium‑priced, integrated combi‑steamer through retail channels, subscription services, or partnerships that emphasize space‑efficiency and convenience.
assumptions: Home cooks prioritize space and convenience over raw cooking performance.
Marketing can effectively communicate the appliance’s versatility and compact design.
The combi‑steamer can be designed to fit standard kitchen layouts without significant modification.
predictions: Home cooks will rank space‑saving as a top purchase criterion when evaluating a combi‑steamer.
Purchase intent will be higher when the product is positioned as a single‑appliance solution versus a multi‑tool kit.
Sales will be concentrated in urban households with limited kitchen space and higher disposable income.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and choice-based conjoint. Participants view a product description of a differentiated combi-steamer and are asked to indicate purchase intent (on a 7-point scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). They also rank importance of convenience, health benefits, space savings, and price.
X1.sample: 400 German households (200 home cooks, 200 non-home cooks) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: importance ranking of convenience, health, space, and price.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be driven primarily by space and versatility claims; willingness to pay will be above €1,200 (20% premium). Importance ranking will place space and versatility higher than convenience and health.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address home cook demand, convenience, or health benefits. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition that emphasizes convenience, health benefits, and modern design, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology. Begin with a limited pilot in high‑income German households to test demand and willingness to pay before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: German households with higher disposable income and exposure to premium kitchen appliances, particularly those seeking efficient, health‑conscious cooking solutions.
final.value_proposition: A premium, smart combi‑steamer that delivers convenience, health benefits (e.g., lower oil use, even cooking), and modern design, sold through direct channels, subscription services, or retail partnerships.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 6‑week online survey test (400 households) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated combi‑steamer framed on convenience and health.
final.uncertainty: The size of the home‑cook market and the exact price premium they are willing to pay remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand from home cooks is lacking; the current B2B focus limits consumer reach.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent below 15% or willingness to pay below €1,200 (20% premium), the recommendation would shift to stay focused on professional kitchens.
If new evidence shows home cooks consistently rank space and versatility as top purchase criteria, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift accordingly.

result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-EPRO-UPDATE shows that emphasizing durability and repairability led to 72 reservations versus 32 for performance‑price, demonstrating that a differentiated proposition can increase purchase intent. This directly supports T1, which predicts that highlighting durability and repairability will drive higher conversion among homeowners.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging the growing residential demand for commercial‑quality home laundry solutions. Begin with a limited pilot offering a compact, self‑service unit priced at a premium but acceptable to consumers, and use online and retail channels to reach the target segment.
arguments.target_customer: Homeowners in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other residential settings who need reliable, commercial‑grade laundry equipment for home use.
arguments.value_proposition: A consumer‑oriented, space‑efficient self‑service unit that delivers professional‑grade washing and drying performance, enabling residents to manage their own laundry with minimal downtime and cost.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Small Business Intent Test (500 respondents, 8‑week survey) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay among homeowners and small businesses. Use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full‑f‑
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the residential market and the price sensitivity of homeowners are uncertain. The test will clarify whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for durability and repairability, which is central to T1.
would_change_if: If the test shows homeowners conversion ≥ 5% and small businesses conversion <8%, we would shift focus to a consumer‑focused proposition for small businesses (T2).
If the test shows small businesses conversion ≥ 8% and homeowners conversion <5%, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore other segments.

If new evidence shows that residential demand is much smaller than expected or that small‑business demand is already high, we would abandon the consumer proposition and focus on existing professional segments.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).

4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and compact design, targeting home baristas who value time efficiency and space savings. Begin with a limited launch of a compact machine priced at €2,000€2,500, using direct‑to‑consumer channels and a marketing campaign that highlights quick brewing and easy storage.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Home baristas value convenience and compact design; they will purchase a new consumer machine if it offers quick brewing and easy storage, even at a premium price.
T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group gains higher-margin sales and brand association with home convenience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Baristas prioritize time efficiency and space savings in small homes or offices; a compact machine reduces setup time and footprint.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing justified by convenience; Simonelli can capture value through direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning as a home convenience leader.
assumptions: Home barista market exists and is willing to pay for convenience.
Simonelli can produce a compact machine without compromising performance.
Marketing can effectively communicate convenience benefits.
predictions: If offered a compact machine priced at €2,000-€2,500, at least 15% of surveyed home baristas will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion rate will be higher than for a standard professional machine of similar price point.

Marketing can effectively communicate quality benefits.
predictions: If offered a premium machine priced at €3,000-€3,500, at least 10% of surveyed home baristas will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
