result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-SIMO-UPDATE shows a structured learning offer increased reservations among home barista enthusiasts, supporting the idea that convenience and skill-building drive purchase decisions. This directly contradicts T2, which predicts premium quality would be the primary driver.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-SIMO-UPDATE shows that a structured learning offer (home-barista lesson) generated 72 reservations compared to 32 for a product-specification orientation. This demonstrates that a social/learning mechanism can drive purchase decisions among enthusiasts, supporting T1 that social interaction drives demand.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes social interaction and community, rather than a purely convenience-focused offering. arguments.target_customer: Home baristas and coffee enthusiasts who value social experiences and community in their coffee preparation.
arguments.value_proposition: A machine that serves as a social hub, enabling friends and family to join in the brewing process, share photos, and build a community around coffee. This positions Simonelli as a premium brand for the social side of home espresso.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure whether participants choose the social-friendly feature over the convenience-friendly feature and are willing to pay a premium for it.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for social-friendly features and Simonelli’s ability to design and price such a product remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether there is sufficient demand to justify investment.
would_change_if: If the test shows the convenience-friendly feature is chosen at a higher rate than the social-friendly feature, or if willingness to pay for convenience features exceeds that for social features, we would reconsider focusing on convenience.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for social features in a broader market, we would strengthen the case for a social-focused proposition.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home baristas with a compact, entry-level espresso machine, leveraging Simonelli’s design expertise to capture premium margins.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Home barista culture will drive demand for compact, entry‑level espresso machines that fit small spaces, creating a consumer segment willing to pay a premium for convenience.
T1.who_benefits: Home baristas seeking consistent espresso at home; Simonelli Group would capture value through premium pricing and brand association with quality coffee.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The pandemic reinforced the home barista lifestyle, and consumers now view espresso as a daily ritual rather than a professional tool. They seek equipment that fits their living spaces and offers consistent results.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can sell compact machines at a higher price point than standard professional models, leveraging its existing design expertise to differentiate and command premium margins.
assumptions: Home barista participation rates will remain stable or increase after pandemic recovery.
Consumers will prioritize space efficiency and ease of use over professional features.
Simonelli can adapt its product line to meet these new requirements without compromising core performance.
predictions: A test offering a compact entry‑level machine will generate at least 20 pre‑orders within 12 weeks at a price 15% above standard professional models.
Surveyed home baristas will rank space and ease of use as top purchase criteria for new equipment.
T1.first_claim: Home barista culture will drive demand for compact, entry‑level espresso machines that fit small spaces, creating a consumer segment willing to pay a premium for convenience.

T2.claim: Professional coffee shop operators will adopt compact, entry‑level espresso machines to reduce space requirements and lower operational costs, creating a consumer segment willing to pay for scalability.
T2.who_benefits: Coffee shops seeking efficient equipment; Simonelli Group would capture value through volume sales and brand association with professional quality.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Smaller spaces and higher rental costs in urban areas push shops to prioritize space‑saving equipment. Entry‑level machines offer consistent espresso without the bulk of full‑size models.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can sell compact machines at a price point below standard professional models, leveraging its existing design to meet shop needs and achieve higher unit volume.
assumptions: Shop operators will consider equipment cost as a key purchase factor.
Compact machines will deliver acceptable espresso quality for daily use.
Simonelli can adapt its product line to meet shop requirements without compromising core performance.
predictions: A test offering a compact machine to 20 professional shops will generate at least 10 pre‑orders within 12 weeks at a price 10% below standard professional models.
Surveyed shop owners will rank space savings and cost efficiency as top purchase criteria for new equipment.
T2.first_claim: Professional coffee shop operators will adopt compact, entry‑level espresso machines to reduce space requirements and lower operational costs, creating a consumer segment willing to pay for scalability.

result.brief: Simonelli Group makes commercial espresso machines and grinders under the Nuova Simonelli and Victoria Arduino brands. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home barista enthusiasts, leveraging Simonelli’s premium professional reputation and limited consumer offerings. Begin with a low‑cost test (e.g., a limited‑edition compact machine) to validate demand before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Home barista culture will sustain demand for premium espresso equipment, allowing Simonelli to capture value through premium pricing and brand positioning.
T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group (through higher margins and brand prestige) and home barista enthusiasts who value quality and social experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Home barista culture emphasizes quality, social interaction, and the third-place experience of cafes, creating a willingness to invest in premium equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can charge premium prices for its high-end machines and grinders, leveraging its professional reputation and limited consumer offerings to differentiate in a slowing prosumer market.
assumptions: Home barista culture remains a significant driver of coffee equipment demand.
Simonelli can effectively communicate the premium value of its products to this segment.
Regulatory and safety concerns do not significantly limit consumer adoption of home espresso equipment.
predictions: If Simonelli launches a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home baristas, it will achieve higher average transaction value than its current professional line.
Surveyed home baristas will express willingness to pay a premium for equipment that aligns with their social and quality expectations.
Simonelli's consumer sales will grow faster than its professional segment in the next 12 months.
T1.first_claim: Home barista culture will sustain demand for premium espresso equipment, allowing Simonelli to capture value through premium pricing and brand positioning.

T2.claim: Coffee shops and hotels will increase demand for compact, easy-to-use espresso equipment, creating a consumer segment that can be served with differentiated offerings.
T2.who_benefits: Simonelli Group (through new product sales and brand extension) and coffee shop/hotel operators seeking efficient, high-quality equipment.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Coffee shops and hotels need equipment that is easy to operate, fits small spaces, and delivers consistent espresso, reducing training costs and increasing throughput.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can sell compact, consumer-friendly machines at a premium price, leveraging its professional reputation to attract these new buyers and capture higher margins.
assumptions: Coffee shop and hotel operators are willing to invest in equipment that improves efficiency and customer experience.
Compact, easy-to-use machines are feasible and meet quality expectations.
Simonelli can adapt its professional expertise to a consumer-focused product line without compromising performance.
predictions: If Simonelli launches a compact consumer proposition targeting coffee shops and hotels, it will achieve higher unit sales than its current professional line in the same segment.
Surveyed shop owners will indicate that equipment ease of use and space efficiency are top purchase criteria.
Simonelli's consumer sales in the coffee shop/hotel segment will grow faster than its professional segment in the next 12 months.

arguments.claim: Home barista culture will sustain demand for premium espresso equipment, allowing Simonelli to capture value through premium pricing and brand positioning.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they seek convenience, health benefits, and premium quality, willing to pay a premium for a single, versatile appliance.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks gain convenience and healthier cooking; RATIONAL benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of health benefits and convenience drives consumers to replace traditional cooking methods with a single, high-performance appliance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a premium price for a differentiated product, leveraging its brand reputation and the convenience of a single appliance.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay more for a single, high-quality cooking solution.
Health and convenience are primary purchase drivers for home cooks.
RATIONAL can differentiate its product through design, smart features, or subscription services.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a combi-steamer compared to a comparable multi-appliance setup.
Pilot sales of a differentiated home-combi-steamer will show higher conversion rates than standard models.
Brand perception studies will rank RATIONAL higher for premium home cooking than for professional kitchens.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they seek convenience, health benefits, and premium quality, willing to pay a premium for a single, versatile appliance.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value sustainability and reduce kitchen waste, seeking eco-friendly appliances that lower long-term costs.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks gain reduced waste and lower utility bills; RATIONAL benefits by positioning as an environmentally responsible brand and potentially offering subscription recycling services.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of environmental impact and desire to reduce single-use kitchen items drives purchase of durable, reusable appliances.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can price a differentiated product at a premium, market it as sustainable, and potentially bundle recycling programs to capture recurring revenue.
assumptions: Home cooks prioritize sustainability over price in appliance choices.
Durability and recyclability are key purchase criteria for eco-conscious consumers.
RATIONAL can design a product that is easily disassembled and recyclable.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will rank sustainability higher than price when choosing a combi-steamer.
Pilot sales of a sustainable-combi-steamer will show higher repeat purchase intent than standard models.
Environmental messaging will increase brand awareness among target home-cook segment.
T2.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer proposition because they value sustainability and reduce kitchen waste, seeking eco-friendly appliances that lower long-term costs.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription-based combi-steamer) targeting convenience, health, and premium design, while maintaining the professional line.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking efficient, health-conscious cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If they perceive the device as a time-saving, health-enhancing tool that also adds aesthetic value to their kitchen, they will purchase it over traditional methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can capture value through premium pricing, subscription services for software updates, and brand positioning as a premium home appliance.
assumptions: Home cooks have sufficient disposable income to invest in a premium kitchen appliance.

The device can be marketed as a lifestyle product rather than just a cooking tool.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition (smart, compact, or subscription-based combi-steamer) targeting convenience, health, and premium design, while maintaining the professional line.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE shows that home cooks prefer a coordinated-installation offer over a purchaser-arranged one, indicating that friction in installation can influence purchase decisions. This directly supports T1, which predicts that convenience and health benefits drive home cooks to choose a differentiated premium proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

update.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
update.note: A new SIMULATED result is available. Read it with read_source.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.
